title: Struggling to breathe — sit them up and get help
applies_to: Someone who is awake but fighting for every breath, can only speak in short bursts, or whose lips look blue.

citations.source: WHO and IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021: First Aid
citations.section: Recognition of breathing difficulty and positioning

steps.text: Ask them to say their name. If they can get out only one or two words, the breathing is very bad.
Call for an ambulance now. Say they are fighting for breath.
Help them sit upright, leaning forward a little, with their arms resting on a table or on their knees.
Open a window or a door. Loosen anything tight around the neck and the chest.
Ask whether they have their own puffer, sometimes called an inhaler, that a doctor gave them for this.
If they do, help them use their own one, exactly as the label on it says.
Speak slowly and keep the room calm. Ask them to breathe out for longer than they breathe in.
Keep watching their lips and their face. Stay with them until help arrives.

do_not: Do not make them lie flat. Lying down makes breathing harder.
Do not leave them alone while you fetch things.
Do not give them anything to eat or drink.
Do not let them use a puffer that belongs to someone else.
Do not crowd them. One calm person close by is better than four.
escalate_if: Their lips, tongue, or face turn blue or grey — say this on the phone at once.
They stop answering you and stop breathing normally — start pushing on the chest.
They go quiet and stop fighting to breathe — that is worse, not better. Tell the crew now.
Their face or throat is swelling too — this may be a bad allergy reaction.
They are holding their chest, or the pain spreads to an arm or the jaw — say so on the phone.
